## Why compose models?

- Named components expose biological assumptions and connections.
- One Catalyst reaction network can generate deterministic and stochastic
  problem types.
- Structure matters: homogeneous mixing hides group-specific contact patterns.

Today: current ModelingToolkit 11 and Catalyst 16 APIs.

::: {.notes}
Composition is an audit tool. Compile and inspect the equations before trusting
the numerical trajectory.
:::

## Symbolic components

For a deterministic continuous-time continuous-state SIR:

$$
\dot S=-\beta SI/N,\qquad
\dot I=\beta SI/N-\gamma I,\qquad
\dot R=\gamma I.
$$

Keep the flows in separate `System` components, connect shared states and
parameters, then call `compose` and `mtkcompile`.

```{julia}
using CairoMakie, ModelingToolkit, OrdinaryDiffEq
using ModelingToolkit: t_nounits as t, D_nounits as D
@variables S(t) I(t) R(t); @parameters β γ
@named s = System([D(S) ~ -β*S*I/(S+I+R)], t)
@named i = System([D(I) ~ β*S*I/(S+I+R)-γ*I], t)
@named r = System([D(R) ~ γ*I], t)
nothing
```

::: {.notes}
The complete connection system is shown in the book and notebook. The key API
is the current `System` → `compose` → `mtkcompile` pipeline.
:::

## Structured mixing as reactions

For two groups, $m_{12}=m_{21}=0.5$ modifies cross-group infection:

$$
\lambda_1=\frac{\beta c_1}{N}(S_1I_1+m_{12}S_1I_2),\quad
\lambda_2=\frac{\beta c_2}{N}(m_{21}S_2I_1+S_2I_2).
$$

```{julia}
using Catalyst
network = @reaction_network begin
    @parameters N
    (β*c1)/N, S1 + I1 --> 2I1
    (β*c1*m12)/N, S1 + I2 --> I1 + I2
    (β*c2*m21)/N, S2 + I1 --> I2 + I1
    (β*c2)/N, S2 + I2 --> 2I2
    γ, I1 --> R1
    γ, I2 --> R2
end
nothing
```

## One network, multiple interpretations

```{julia}
using OrdinaryDiffEq, StochasticDiffEq, JumpProcesses
u0 = [:S1=>495.0,:I1=>5.0,:R1=>0.0,:S2=>495.0,:I2=>5.0,:R2=>0.0]
p = [:N=>1000.0,:β=>0.05,:c1=>10.0,:c2=>10.0,
     :m12=>0.5,:m21=>0.5,:γ=>0.25]
ode = solve(ODEProblem(network,u0,(0.0,2.0),p), Tsit5(); saveat=0.05)
nothing
```

The same `ReactionSystem` can be passed to an `SDEProblem` (chemical-Langevin
approximation) or `JumpProblem` (integer-count event process). Their state
spaces and error claims are different.

## Generated comparison

```{julia}
#| fig-cap: "Aggregate infectious prevalence generated from the structured reaction-network model."
fig = Figure(size=(800,350))
ax = Axis(fig[1,1], xlabel="time", ylabel="I₁ + I₂")
lines!(ax, ode.t, ode[:I1] .+ ode[:I2], label="structured ODE")
axislegend(ax)
fig
```

Validation: the ODE and jump stoichiometry conserve
$S_1+I_1+R_1+S_2+I_2+R_2$. A Gaussian SDE can leave the nonnegative domain;
report that diagnostic rather than clipping it silently.

## Takeaways and links

- Use `System`, `compose`, and `mtkcompile` for inspectable symbolic assembly.
- Use Catalyst reactions to preserve stoichiometry and reuse a model.
- Group structure introduces parameters that aggregate incidence may not identify.

Read the [book appendix](../../appendices/09-model-composition.html),
[ModelingToolkit composition](https://docs.sciml.ai/ModelingToolkit/stable/basics/Composition/),
and [Catalyst system generation](https://catalyst.sciml.ai/stable/manual/systems/).

::: {.notes}
Do not equate ODE, SDE, and jump trajectories. They are related model
interpretations with different state spaces, noise, and validation requirements.
:::
